newsitem.title: CANADA: GM Canada union meets secret plant buyer.
newsitem.headline: GM Canada union meets secret plant buyer.

text.p: Canadian Auto Workers union president Buzz Hargrove said General Motors Corp's Canadian subsidiary insisted he meet with the chief executive officer of a secret buyer for two of its parts plants in Canada.

The leader of Canada's largest private sector union said he told the CEO of "Newco" that he could buy four GM parts plants including a fabrication plant in Oshawa, Ontario and a trim plant in Windsor, but that the union would insist the employees are covered by its master labor agreement with GM.
"I told him you can buy if you want, you buy us, but you also buy the CAW-GM master collective agreement," he said.

Hargrove said the union would insist on making a deal similar to its agreement with American Axle, which bought GM's axle plant in St. Catharines, Ontario three years ago. Although it is considered a separate company by GM, American Axle's workers are covered by the union's agreement with GM.
Sources close to the talks hinted that "Newco" may be a U.S. Wall Street investment firm named Joseph, Littlejohn & Levy, a private investment partnership.
"I can't tell you who it is, but I can say it is a U.S. investment firm and the executive is an American," the source said.

Reuters reported on September 6 that General Motors refused to confirm reports in the Oakland Press in Pontiac, Michigan that Joseph, Littlejohn and Levy was negotiating to buy four parts plants from GM.
GM has said it intends to sell interior components plants in Livonia and Flint, Michigan as a package deal that includes the Oshawa and Windsor plants in Canada.
The CAW began negotiating with General Motors of Canada Ltd for a new collective labor agreement on Monday, one day after ratifying a groundbreaking deal with Chrysler Corp's Canadian subsidiary.

The union had said it intends to reverse GM's outsourcing decisions along the lines of its deal with Chrysler, which set down a moratorium on plant closures and sales and committed the company to refrain from reducing jobs through outsourcing.
"They will accept the Chrysler pattern," Hargrove said.

Traditionally the Canadian Auto Workers union sets an established pattern at the first car company it negotiates with and then applies that deal to the other two subsidiaries of big North American auto companies.
Spokesmen for General Motors were unavailable for comment.
